cards.note: In the southern half of Germany many Towns/villages use the -ach ending
In the eastern part of Germany many Towns/villages use the -itz ending
In the north-eastern part of Germany many Towns/villages use the -ow ending

While most of Germany uses B-Type guardrails, some regions predominantly use A-Type instead. Learning which regions use them can be useful.

NOTE: There will always be rare exceptions. For a good overview of European guardrails, see this infographic.
There are two regional Aldi chains, which have split Germany in two; Aldi Süd in the south, and Aldi Nord in the north.
Covers most of North Rhine-Westphalia, northern Rhineland-Palatinate, and parts of Hesse. NOTE: Area codes starting with 01 are mobile and therefore not region-specific.
Includes Berlin, Brandenburg, Saxony, Thuringia, and parts of Saxony-Anhalt. NOTE: Area codes starting with 01 are mobile and therefore not region-specific.
Covers Hamburg, Bremen, Schleswig-Holstein, and coastal Lower Saxony. NOTE: Area codes starting with 01 are mobile and therefore not region-specific.
Includes Lower Saxony, northern Hesse, and parts of North Rhine-Westphalia. NOTE: Area codes starting with 01 are mobile and therefore not region-specific.
Covers Saarland, Rhineland-Palatinate, central and southern Hesse, and parts of Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg. NOTE: Area codes starting with 01 are mobile and therefore not region-specific.
Includes most of Baden-Württemberg and parts of Rhineland-Palatinate and Bavaria. NOTE: Area codes starting with 01 are mobile and therefore not region-specific.
Covers southern Bavaria. NOTE: Area codes starting with 01 are mobile and therefore not region-specific.
Includes northern Bavaria, parts of Thuringia, Hesse, and Baden-Württemberg. NOTE: Area codes starting with 01 are mobile and therefore not region-specific.
In Germany there are both B-/ and A-Type Guardrail. Learning which regions can be useful.
Baden-Württemberg uses this grey desgin with white plates on its triangular posts. NOTE: The grey colour can be washed out and the post can look white
Similarly, Baden-Württemberg is the only state where the plates on the bollards can be grey instead of white. They also can freature two black stripes at the top and bottom.
Bavaria uses these white rectangular road markers, which are divided by black lines into three sections. The left section provides the road you are currently on.
These round wooden bollards, which have a painted top, are found in Bavaria.
Bavarian churches often have a rounded top on the tower. NOTE: This can be found in BW rarely.
Berlin uses segmented bus stops, with a yellow signpost. Its often seen together with the trash bin.
Berlin uses white signs with a grey border, and a separate section for numbers under the street name. Also note how the letter ß looks.
Berlin uses bright orange bins that have white text on them. Its often seen together with the bus stop.
Bielefeld has these yellow bands around they´re stop lights all over the city.
In rural central-southern parts of the Black Forest you can find this pretty unique architecture with often low roofs and long balconies.
Some bollards in North Rhine-Westphalia have a green bit at the top. The top can also be another colour.
Fully yellow posts are found in the state of Brandenburg.
Bremen proper uses simple bus stops, which have the bus stop name within a red section. The edges can be rounded. Its often seen together with the trash bin.
Bremen has green and grey bins, with orange speech bubbles. Its often seen together with the bus stop sign.
Bremerhaven trash bins use a more generic green design, with a black logo. Its often seen together with the bus stop sign.

Bremerhaven, which is still part of Bremen, uses bus stops with a grey section on the opposite side of the signpost. And the bus stop name is red within a yellow section. Its often seen together with the trash bin.

Lampposts in Cologne will often feature these bright yellow numbers on a black piece of plastic.

NOTE: Similar looking things can be found elsewhere as well.
These large, utilitarian apartment buildings constructed during the socialist era, that are also known as “Commie blocks” are common in all of former East Germany.
Dortmund uses different blue variants in a grey frame, but the sign has a seperate section for numbers.
Dresden has blue street signs with a unique font.
Fristo is a drink market chain. Its common in the south half and the east of Germany, its easy recognizable with its unique sign being often visible from roads.
This round concrete pole with metal straps around it is most common in Saxony but also generally in eastern Germany.
Concrete Pole with split bar on top. The middle part is thicker and the insulators are a little bit longer and thicker. NOTE: this can be confused with other Poles existing everywhere!
The German Alps is the most mountainous region in Germany, it is mostly concentrated on the Austrian Border.
Many trees in Brandenburg and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern have these tiny green markers on them. You can very rarely find them in Lower Saxony.
This type of half-timbered house with arches at the ground floor is very common in this region of Saxony.
Hamburg bus stops have a red signpost, and the route numbers are within hexagons. Note that they can be found outside of Hamburg as well. They are often seen together with the trash bin.
Hamburg uses bright red bins, with white speech bubbles. Also they are most often seen with the bus stop.
Hop is are most common seen above Munich. Also there is a dense area above "Friedrichshafen" above the Lake of Constance.
A Loop ending of the guardrail is common in Brandenburg, Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania (especially in brandenburg)
**Lowcam **coverage can be found around Singen and near Switzerland.
Some of the green caps will have the text ‘LVR’, along with a small coat of arms. These specific green caps are unique to southern North Rhine-Westphalia.

Magdeburg uses green-(orange)-white trams and busses. They have "MVB" (Magdeburger Verkehrs Betriebe) in a special font on them. Trams can freature large ads. NOTE: They can be red but will always have the "MVB" on them.
Mainz has a mix of blue signs, and this unique red variant.
Munich uses specific Bus Stops. They commonly have this blue design with the rounded top, on boards to each side it displays the stops name which can be used to regionguess.
Munich has blue street signs with a white decorative border that does not touch the corners. Also note the unique font. NOTE: While the blue design itsself is common elsewhere the font is unique
The area around Munich (13 Lkr.) use a unique blue bus stop design with a green frame and MVV written on its bottom. NOTE: not common in the city of Munich

Munich uses specific trams/busses they most commoly have a

  • blue design and have the name of the public transport company
  • "MVG" printed on them.
  • In they front they often show the Munich coat of arms.
  • The trams can have large ads on them.

These brick houses are generally concentrated in northwestern Germany.

NOTE: This map is very approximate.
North Rhine-Westphalia can use these unique sign posts for pedestrian crossings. NOTE: They are rare but unique
North Rhine-Westphalia uses white posts without white plates on the sides. You can also find posts which go all the way to the ground.

These irregular looking bollards, which do not have a white encasing on the bottom half, are found on K-roads in this region of Lower Saxony. K-Roads in this region will not have any other type of bollard.

Baltic Pines or Pinus sylvestris are generally more concentrated in the northeast of Germany. They can be recognized by their orange-tinged trunk.

NOTE: This map is very approximate.

Covers Hamburg, Schleswig-Holstein, northern Lower Saxony, Bremen, and a small part of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Includes southern Lower Saxony, eastern North Rhine-Westphalia, northern Hesse, Thuringia, and parts of Saxony-Anhalt.
Used in northwestern North Rhine-Westphalia and southwestern Lower Saxony.
Covers southwestern North Rhine-Westphalia, large parts of Rhineland-Palatinate, and parts of Hesse.
Includes southern Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland, and small parts of Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.
Covers most of Baden-Württemberg and small areas of Rhineland-Palatinate.
Found in southern Bavaria and the southeastern part of Baden-Württemberg.

These white posts with a red cap are found in all of former East Germany, but most commonly in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.
North Rhine-Westphalia & Hamburg are using a red cycling sign desing.
The flat plains southeast of Regensburg can be recognised by the slight ridge often visible to the northeast. The plains themselves are flat, and quite agricultural.
Rhineland-Palatinate is the only state where the plates on the bollards are orange instead of white.
Saarland uses a green cycling sign.
This red bollard can rarely be found in Saxony-Anhalt.

Yellow posts with a white plate on them are found in Saxony-Anhalt.

NOTE: Sometimes there is only 1 plate, which can make it hard to tell apart from a Brandenburg post.
Thatched roofs and rock walls are most common on the North Frisian Islands, as well as mainland Schleswig-Holstein. You can also commonly find them in coastal resort towns in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

You can use the sign back connectors on street signs to regionguess Germany.

NOTE: The double connector on triangular signs are generally wider. T-shaped connectors may look like this.

You can use the sign backs of street signs to regionguess Germany.

Here are examples of a folded, and flat sign back.
These simple orange posts are most commonly found in Bavaria, and also in the other highlighted states.
Houses with black slate walls, resembling fish scales, are commonly found in a large area of central Germany.
Sorbian, a Slavic language, is spoken near the Polish and Czech border. You can find it on a variety of signs in these regions.
In the south of the country you can find big houses with traditional wooden details, often featuring balconies with flowers.
In the entire city of Stuttgart, there are a lot of roads with these kind off tram rails in the middle.
The suffix "-beck" can be found in the northern half of the country
In the north(west) of Schleswig-Holstein right next to the Danish border, 30 places use the suffix "-büll" in their name.
In the north(east) of Schleswig-Holstein, 49 places use the suffix "-by" in their names.
The suffix "-hofen" can be found in the southern half of the country.
In the west of NRW, parts of Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland, 144 places use the suffix "-rath" in their name.
The suffix "-ried" can be found in some parts of the southern half of the country.
There are 124 places using the suffix "-roth"
In NRW, parts of Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland, 195 places use the suffix "-scheid" in their name. NOTE: there 3 of them elsewhere.
The suffix "-stetten" is can be found in the southern half of the country
In the area southwest of Düsseldorf and around Bonn you can find 36 places using the suffix "hoven"

The shrub and sand covered hills are unique to the island of Sylt. And like the rest of the North Frisian Islands, rock walls, brick houses, and thatched roofs are common.

NOTE: Some parts of Sylt look more generic, but still very flat.
Vineyards are mostly concentrated in the southwest of Germany. However, there are a couple regions as well. So if there are wineyards you are most likely not far away from Rhine River.
In the southwest of Germany many Towns/villages use "Weiler" in their names. For small villages these signs are sometimes yellow on green and for bigger black on yellow.
Orange/brownish brick can be found west of Mannheim (to the french border)

You can find this rare white and black Generation 4 car in Hamburg and around Frankfurt.

NOTE: You can also find the same car around London and in Ireland.

You can spot trees that are painted white close to the bottom of the trunk in the northeast.

NOTE: You will rarely find them outside the shaded region.
These wooden shingles are called "Schindeln" they are common on older farmshouses or other traditional build houses in southgermany.
